subject: physics
topicDisplay: Unit 10: Electric Force, Field, and Potential (part 1)
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 10.2 Conservation of Electric Charge and the Process of Charging

questions.q: A copper coin is electrically neutral. Which statement correctly describes the charged particles in the coin?
options: It contains no charged particles, because it has no net charge.
It contains more electrons than protons, as an electron has less charge.
It contains huge numbers of protons and electrons, in equal numbers.
It contains protons whose charge is balanced by its many neutrons.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a neutral object contains no charge picks this. 'Neutral' means that the net charge is zero, not that charge is absent: the coin's atoms contain protons and electrons in equal numbers.

A student who thinks the lighter electron carries less charge than the proton picks this, reasoning that extra electrons are needed to balance the protons. The electron's charge (−e) and the proton's (+e) have equal magnitudes, so a neutral object has equal numbers of each.

Charge is a property of the particles that make up all matter. Every copper atom contains 29 protons (+e each) and, in a neutral atom, 29 electrons (−e each), so the coin holds an enormous number of charged particles. They are equal in number, so the net charge is zero.

A student who thinks neutrons cancel the charge of protons picks this. A neutron has no charge, so it cannot balance anything; the positive charge of the protons is balanced by the negative charge of an equal number of electrons.
questions.explain: Charge is a property of the particles that make up all matter. Every copper atom contains 29 protons (+e each) and, in a neutral atom, 29 electrons (−e each), so the coin holds an enormous number of charged particles. They are equal in number, so the net charge is zero.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. At the level of atoms, which statement explains why the book does not fall through the table?
options: Electric forces between the charged particles of the two surfaces push the book up.
The table is solid, so it blocks the book without exerting any force on the book.
The book's weight comes back up from the table as a reaction to Earth's gravity.
A fundamental contact force, unrelated to charge, acts wherever surfaces touch.
optionWhy: The book presses the surface atoms of the table slightly closer together, and the electric forces between the electrons and nuclei in the two surfaces push the book upward. This combined electric push is what we call the normal force, a contact force.

A student who thinks a support only gets in the way picks this. Without an upward force the book would accelerate downward; the table exerts that force, which comes from electric forces between the particles of the two surfaces.

A student who thinks the table's push is the book's weight returned as a reaction picks this. The weight is exerted on the book by Earth; the table's push is a separate force with an electric origin, and it is not the third-law partner of the weight.

A student who thinks contact forces are a separate fundamental force picks this. Contact forces are not fundamental: they are the combined effect of electric forces between enormous numbers of charged particles in the surfaces.
questions.explain: The book presses the surface atoms of the table slightly closer together, and the electric forces between the electrons and nuclei in the two surfaces push the book upward. This combined electric push is what we call the normal force, a contact force.

questions.q: Two electrons are held a short distance apart, far from all other objects. Which statement correctly describes the forces the electrons exert on each other?
options: They exert repulsive forces of both kinds, as their charges are alike.
Each electron repels the other electrically and attracts it gravitationally.
They exert only repulsive electric forces, having too little mass for gravity.
Their gravitational attraction exceeds their electric repulsion.
optionWhy: A student who thinks gravitational forces follow the signs of the charges picks this. Gravitational forces depend on mass, not charge, and are always attractive.

The electrons have charges of the same sign, so their electric forces are repulsive. They also have mass, and gravitational forces are always attractive. Both forces act, in opposite directions; the electric force is by far the larger.

A student who thinks only large bodies exert gravitational forces picks this. Any two objects with mass attract each other gravitationally; between electrons the force is extremely small, but it acts.
A student who thinks gravity is the stronger force picks this. For two electrons the electric repulsion is about 10⁴² times the gravitational attraction, so the electrons push each other apart.
questions.explain: The electrons have charges of the same sign, so their electric forces are repulsive. They also have mass, and gravitational forces are always attractive. Both forces act, in opposite directions; the electric force is by far the larger.

questions.q: The electric force between two protons is far greater than the gravitational force between them. Why, then, is the motion of the planets around the Sun governed by gravitational forces rather than electric forces?
options: The Sun and planets are almost exactly neutral, so their electric forces nearly cancel.
Electric forces die out over short distances, but gravitational forces do not.
Electric forces cannot act across the vacuum of space that separates these bodies.
Their enormous masses make gravity stronger than any electric force they could have.
optionWhy: Large bodies contain almost equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so the electric forces of their particles nearly cancel. The gravitational forces of all their particles are attractive and add up, so gravity dominates at large scales even though it is the weaker force between particles.

A student who thinks electric forces act only at short range picks this. Both forces decrease as 1/r² and neither dies out; the electric forces between the Sun and planets are small only because the bodies are nearly neutral.

A student who thinks electric forces need a material to pass through picks this. Electric forces act across empty space, as gravitational forces do; Coulomb's law with ε₀ describes charges in free space.

A student who explains the dominance of gravity by mass alone picks this. If the Sun and planets carried even a tiny fraction of their particles' charge as net charge, the electric forces would far exceed gravity; gravity wins because they are almost neutral.
questions.explain: Large bodies contain almost equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so the electric forces of their particles nearly cancel. The gravitational forces of all their particles are attractive and add up, so gravity dominates at large scales even though it is the weaker force between particles.

questions.q: A plastic rod and a wool cloth, both initially neutral, are rubbed together. Afterward the rod is negatively charged. Which statement describes what happened during the rubbing?
options: Protons moved from the rod across to the wool.
Rubbing made new electrons on the rod's surface.
Electrons moved off the rod and over to the wool.
Electrons moved from the wool onto the rod.
optionWhy: A student who thinks positive charges move during charging picks this. Protons are held in the atomic nuclei and do not move from one solid to another when they are rubbed; the rod became negative by gaining electrons.
A student who thinks rubbing makes charge picks this. Charge is never created: the extra electrons on the rod came from the wool, which is left positively charged by the same amount.

A student who links 'negative' with losing something picks this. Electrons are negative, so an object that loses them becomes positive. The rod became negative, so it must have gained electrons, from the wool.
Charging a solid moves electrons. The rod ends up with more electrons than protons, so it is negative; the wool has lost the same number of electrons, so it is positive by the same amount.
questions.explain: Charging a solid moves electrons. The rod ends up with more electrons than protons, so it is negative; the wool has lost the same number of electrons, so it is positive by the same amount.

questions.q: A metal sphere on an insulating stand has a charge of +5.0 nC. It is then connected to Earth by a metal wire, with no other charged objects nearby. Which statement describes what happens?
options: Positive charge flows off the sphere and down the wire into the Earth.
Charge flows until the sphere and the Earth hold equal amounts of charge.
No charge flows, as the neutral Earth exerts no electric force.
Electrons flow from Earth onto the sphere until it is almost neutral.
optionWhy: A student who thinks positive charges move in metals picks this. The protons stay in the nuclei of the sphere's atoms; the sphere loses its positive charge because electrons flow onto it from Earth.

A student who thinks objects in contact always end with equal charges picks this. Equal sharing holds only for identical conductors. Earth is enormous compared with the sphere, so the sphere ends nearly neutral and Earth's charge barely changes.

A student who thinks a neutral object cannot interact with a charged one picks this. Earth contains vast numbers of electrons, and the positive sphere attracts them: once the wire connects the two, electrons flow onto the sphere.

The sphere has fewer electrons than protons. When it is connected to Earth, a very large, approximately neutral object, electrons flow up the wire onto the sphere until almost none of its excess charge is left. Earth's own charge hardly changes, because Earth is so large.
questions.explain: The sphere has fewer electrons than protons. When it is connected to Earth, a very large, approximately neutral object, electrons flow up the wire onto the sphere until almost none of its excess charge is left. Earth's own charge hardly changes, because Earth is so large.

questions.q: A negatively charged rod is held near the metal knob at the top of an electroscope that has no net charge, without touching it. The electroscope's two thin metal leaves spread apart. Which statement describes the charge in the electroscope while the rod is held there?
options: The whole electroscope has now become negatively charged, like the rod.
The rod's presence has made new negative charge appear on the leaves.
Electrons have been pushed from the knob down onto the pair of leaves.
Positive charges have moved up from the leaves into the knob.
optionWhy: A student who thinks an object near a charged rod takes on the rod's sign picks this. The rod does not touch the electroscope, so no charge passes to it and its net charge stays zero. The rod only moves electrons within it: the leaves become negative and the knob becomes positive by the same amount.

A student who thinks charging makes new charge picks this. Charge is never created. The negative charge on the leaves consists of electrons that were already in the electroscope and have been pushed down from the knob, which is left positive by the same amount.

The rod's negative charge repels the free electrons in the metal. Some move from the knob down to the leaves, so the leaves carry excess negative charge and repel each other, while the knob is left with an equal positive charge. No charge enters or leaves the electroscope, so its net charge is still zero.

A student who thinks positive charges move in a metal picks this. The protons are fixed in the atomic nuclei; only electrons move. The knob becomes positive because electrons have left it for the leaves, not because positive charge has arrived.
questions.explain: The rod's negative charge repels the free electrons in the metal. Some move from the knob down to the leaves, so the leaves carry excess negative charge and repel each other, while the knob is left with an equal positive charge. No charge enters or leaves the electroscope, so its net charge is still zero.

questions.q: Two identical small metal spheres, X and Y, are mounted on insulating stands. The diagram shows the charge on each sphere. The spheres are touched together and then separated. What is the charge on Y afterward?
optionWhy: A student who adds the charges' sizes and ignores their signs picks this: (8.0 nC + 2.0 nC)/2 = 5.0 nC. Y's charge is negative, so it reduces the total: (+8.0 nC − 2.0 nC)/2 = +3.0 nC.

The total charge is (+8.0 nC) + (−2.0 nC) = +6.0 nC. Charge is conserved, and two identical conducting spheres share it equally, so each ends with +6.0 nC/2 = +3.0 nC. Electrons moved from Y to X until the charges were equal.

A student who thinks each sphere ends up with the whole charge picks this. The +6.0 nC total is shared, not copied: if each sphere had +6.0 nC, the pair would have +12.0 nC, more than it started with. Each has +3.0 nC.

A student who thinks charge moves only when objects are rubbed picks this. Charge moves between conductors that simply touch: here electrons move from Y to X until the two identical spheres carry equal charges.
questions.explain: The total charge is (+8.0 nC) + (−2.0 nC) = +6.0 nC. Charge is conserved, and two identical conducting spheres share it equally, so each ends with +6.0 nC/2 = +3.0 nC. Electrons moved from Y to X until the charges were equal.
questions.working: Total charge before contact: (+8.0 nC) + (−2.0 nC) = +6.0 nC. Charge is conserved, and identical conducting spheres share the total equally: each ends with (+6.0 nC)/2 = +3.0 nC.

questions.q: A small sphere with a positive charge is fixed in place, far from any other charged object. Which statement about the electric field produced by the sphere is correct?
options: It comes into being at a point only when a second charge is placed at that point.
It exists along the field lines drawn from the sphere but not in between them.
It needs air or some other material around the sphere to pass it along.
It exists at points around the sphere even where no other charge is present.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a field needs a charge to be present picks this. The sphere's field exists around it all the time; a second charge placed at a point experiences a force because the field is already there.

A student who reads field lines as the only places where the field exists picks this. Field lines are a model: only a few are drawn, and the field exists at every point around the sphere, including between the lines.
A student who thinks a field needs a material to travel through picks this. Electric fields exist in a vacuum; electric forces act across empty space, for example between the particles of an atom.

A charged object produces an electric field in the space around it. The field has a magnitude and direction at every point, whether or not a charge is there; a charge placed at a point only reveals the field by experiencing a force.
questions.explain: A charged object produces an electric field in the space around it. The field has a magnitude and direction at every point, whether or not a charge is there; a charge placed at a point only reveals the field by experiencing a force.

questions.q: A small sphere with a negative charge is isolated, far from other charged objects. Point P lies due east of the sphere. What is the direction of the electric field produced by the sphere at P?
options: East, away from the sphere, since a field points outward
West, pointing toward the sphere, as the sphere is negative
Either way, depending on the sign of a charge put at P
Neither way: no field exists at P until a charge is put there
optionWhy: A student who thinks every field points away from its source picks this. That is true for a positive charge. A positive test charge at P would be pulled toward the negative sphere, so the field points toward it, west.

The field at a point has the direction of the force on a positive test charge there. A positive test charge at P would be attracted toward the negative sphere, so the field at P points west, toward the sphere.

A student who mixes up the field with the force on a charge picks this. The force on a charge at P depends on its sign, but the field is set by the sphere alone and points toward it, west, whatever is placed at P.
A student who thinks a field needs a charge to be present picks this. The sphere produces a field at P whether or not anything is placed there; the field points west, toward the negative sphere.
questions.explain: The field at a point has the direction of the force on a positive test charge there. A positive test charge at P would be attracted toward the negative sphere, so the field at P points west, toward the sphere.

questions.q: A solid metal sphere on an insulating stand is touched at one point by a negatively charged rod, which leaves excess electrons on it. Once the sphere has reached electrostatic equilibrium, where is its excess charge?
options: Spread evenly through the whole of the sphere's volume
Gathered together at the very center of the sphere
Still at the point where the rod touched the sphere
Spread over the outer surface of the sphere
optionWhy: A student who pictures charge soaking into a conductor picks this. Charges spread through the volume would produce a field inside the metal and push one another outward; they move until they are all on the surface.

A student who takes the point-charge model literally picks this. The field outside the sphere is calculated as if the charge were at the center, but the excess electrons repel one another and end up on the surface, as far apart as possible.
A student who thinks charge stays where it is put picks this. That happens on an insulator. In a metal the excess electrons move freely and repel one another, so they spread over the whole surface.

The excess electrons repel one another and move freely through the metal, so they spread out as far as they can. In electrostatic equilibrium all the excess charge is on the sphere's outer surface, and the field inside the metal is zero.
questions.explain: The excess electrons repel one another and move freely through the metal, so they spread out as far as they can. In electrostatic equilibrium all the excess charge is on the sphere's outer surface, and the field inside the metal is zero.

questions.q: Two small spheres, each with a positive charge, start very far apart. Sphere 1 is held fixed while an external force slowly pushes sphere 2 toward it and then holds sphere 2 at rest a distance r from sphere 1. Which statement about the electric potential energy U_E at the end is correct?
options: U_E of the two-sphere system equals the positive work done by the external force.
U_E of the two-sphere system equals the work done on sphere 2 by the electric force.
U_E of the two-sphere system is negative, since the spheres were brought closer together.
U_E is stored in sphere 2 alone, since sphere 2 is the only sphere that was moved.
optionWhy: U_E is zero when the spheres are infinitely far apart. The spheres repel, so the external force pushes sphere 2 in the direction it moves and does positive work; because sphere 2 gains no kinetic energy, all of this work is stored as the electric potential energy of the two-sphere system.

A student who links U_E to the work of the electric force picks this. The electric force on sphere 2 points away from sphere 1, opposite to the motion, so its work is negative; U_E equals the external force's positive work, which is the same size with the opposite sign.

A student who expects potential energy to fall as objects come together, as it does for gravity, picks this. These charges repel: work had to be done to push them together, so U_E rose from zero and is positive.

A student who assigns potential energy to one object picks this. U_E = k(q₁q₂/r) depends on both charges and on the distance between them: it belongs to the system of the two spheres, whichever sphere was moved.
questions.explain: U_E is zero when the spheres are infinitely far apart. The spheres repel, so the external force pushes sphere 2 in the direction it moves and does positive work; because sphere 2 gains no kinetic energy, all of this work is stored as the electric potential energy of the two-sphere system.

questions.q: A particle with charge +4.0 μC and a particle with charge −5.0 μC are 0.60 m apart. What is the electric potential energy of the two-particle system? Use k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
optionWhy: A student who uses the magnitudes of the charges picks this. U_E = k(q₁q₂/r) takes the charges with their signs: the product (+4.0 μC)(−5.0 μC) is negative, so U_E is −0.30 J.

A student who uses the Coulomb's-law expression k|q₁q₂|/r² for the energy picks this: (9.0 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁶)(5.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.60)² = 0.50. That expression gives the magnitude of the force, in newtons. Electric potential energy is k(q₁q₂/r), with the signs of the charges and r to the first power, giving −0.30 J.

A student who gives each particle its own share of the interaction energy and adds them picks this, counting the one pair twice. A pair of charges has a single interaction energy, k(q₁q₂/r) = −0.30 J.
U_E = k(q₁q₂/r) = (9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)(4.0 × 10⁻⁶ C)(−5.0 × 10⁻⁶ C)/(0.60 m) = −0.30 J. It is negative because the charges have opposite signs.
questions.explain: U_E = k(q₁q₂/r) = (9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)(4.0 × 10⁻⁶ C)(−5.0 × 10⁻⁶ C)/(0.60 m) = −0.30 J. It is negative because the charges have opposite signs.

questions.q: Two particles with charges of the same sign form a system whose electric potential energy is U₀. One particle is replaced by a particle with a charge of the same magnitude but the opposite sign, and the distance between the particles is halved. What is the new electric potential energy of the system?
optionWhy: A student who ignores the signs of the charges picks this, keeping only the effect of the smaller distance. Replacing a charge with one of the opposite sign turns a repelling pair into an attracting one, so U_E becomes negative.
U_E = k(q₁q₂/r). Reversing the sign of one charge reverses the sign of q₁q₂, a factor of −1; halving r doubles 1/r, a factor of 2. The new energy is (−1)(2)U₀ = −2.00U₀.

A student who uses the Coulomb's-law expression k|q₁q₂|/r² for the energy picks this: the absolute values hide the change of sign, and halving r quadruples 1/r². U_E = k(q₁q₂/r) keeps the signs, so the energy becomes negative, and it depends on 1/r, so halving r only doubles its magnitude: −2.00U₀.

A student who takes U_E to be proportional to the separation, as U_g = mgh is to height, picks this. U_E = k(q₁q₂/r) has r in the denominator, so a smaller separation gives a larger magnitude, not a smaller one.
questions.explain: U_E = k(q₁q₂/r). Reversing the sign of one charge reverses the sign of q₁q₂, a factor of −1; halving r doubles 1/r, a factor of 2. The new energy is (−1)(2)U₀ = −2.00U₀.

questions.q: The electric potential at point P, produced by nearby fixed charged objects, is +50 V. Which statement correctly interprets this value?
options: A particle of charge q placed at P adds U_E = q(50 V) to the system.
Any charged particle placed at P has 50 J of electric potential energy.
The electric field produced at P by the objects is 50 V/m.
P has no electric potential until a charge is placed there.
optionWhy: Potential is electric potential energy per unit charge. With a charge q at P, the system's electric potential energy is U_E = qV = q(50 V), which is 50 J for every coulomb of charge placed there.
A student who treats the potential as the energy of whatever is placed at P picks this. 50 V means 50 J per coulomb: a particle of charge q gives U_E = q(50 V), which depends on q.
A student who takes the potential's value as the field's magnitude picks this. The field depends on how the potential changes near P, |ΔV/Δr|, which the value 50 V at one point does not give.
A student who thinks a potential needs a charge at the point picks this. The fixed charged objects produce the potential at P whether or not anything is there; a charge placed at P only reveals it.
questions.explain: Potential is electric potential energy per unit charge. With a charge q at P, the system's electric potential energy is U_E = qV = q(50 V), which is 50 J for every coulomb of charge placed there.
questions.working: V = U_E/q, so U_E = qV = q(+50 V) = (50 J/C)q.

questions.q: Which statement best describes how a battery maintains a potential difference between its terminals?
options: Chemical reactions make new charge, which then collects at the two terminals.
A store of charge put in when it was made keeps its terminals charged until used up.
It pushes out a fixed current, and the potential difference follows from that current.
Chemical reactions move positive and negative charge apart, to opposite terminals.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a battery produces charge picks this. Charge is conserved: the reactions separate existing charge; they do not create it.
A student who pictures a battery as a container of charge picks this. The battery keeps separating charge chemically; what runs down is the chemical energy available, not a supply of charge.
A student who treats a battery as a constant-current source picks this. A battery maintains a potential difference; the current it delivers depends on what is connected to it.

The chemical processes in the battery separate charge that is already present, building up positive charge at one terminal and negative charge at the other. That separation of charge is what produces the potential difference.
questions.explain: The chemical processes in the battery separate charge that is already present, building up positive charge at one terminal and negative charge at the other. That separation of charge is what produces the potential difference.

questions.q: Two metal spheres of different radii are far apart. One is charged and the other is uncharged. They are then connected by a long thin conducting wire. After the charges stop moving, which quantity is the same for the two spheres?
options: The electric potential at the surface of each sphere
The amount of excess charge on each of the two spheres
The excess charge per unit area of each sphere's surface
The magnitude of the electric field just outside each sphere
optionWhy: Electrons move through the wire as long as there is a potential difference between the spheres. They stop when the surfaces are at the same potential, which is the equilibrium condition for conductors in contact.

A student who thinks connected conductors share charge equally picks this. Charge moves until the potentials are equal; spheres of different radii then carry different charges, the larger sphere the larger charge.

A student who thinks the charge spreads evenly over the combined surface picks this. Equal potentials, not equal charge per unit area, set the final state; the smaller sphere ends with the greater charge per unit area.

A student who expects charge flow to stop when the fields balance picks this. Charge moves between the spheres while there is a potential difference between them, so the potentials become equal; the fields outside the two spheres differ.
questions.explain: Electrons move through the wire as long as there is a potential difference between the spheres. They stop when the surfaces are at the same potential, which is the equilibrium condition for conductors in contact.

questions.q: An electron moves from point X to point Y in an electric field. The electric potential at Y is lower than at X. Which statement about the change ΔU_E in the electric potential energy of the electron–field system is correct?
options: ΔU_E is negative, since the electron moves to a lower potential.
ΔU_E is zero, since the energy of the system must be conserved.
ΔU_E is positive, since the charge and ΔV are both negative.
ΔU_E depends on the path the electron takes from X to Y.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a move to a lower potential always lowers the potential energy picks this. That holds for a positive charge. For a negative charge, ΔU_E = qΔV is positive when ΔV is negative.

A student who thinks conservation of energy keeps each form of energy fixed picks this. The total energy is what is conserved; U_E can change as long as another form, such as the electron's kinetic energy, changes to compensate.

ΔU_E = qΔV. The electron's charge is negative, and ΔV = V_Y − V_X is negative because Y is at the lower potential. The product of two negative numbers is positive, so the electric potential energy of the system increases.
A student who thinks ΔU_E depends on the route picks this. ΔU_E = qΔV depends only on the potentials at X and Y, so every path between them gives the same ΔU_E.
questions.explain: ΔU_E = qΔV. The electron's charge is negative, and ΔV = V_Y − V_X is negative because Y is at the lower potential. The product of two negative numbers is positive, so the electric potential energy of the system increases.

questions.q: A particle with charge −q (where q > 0) moves from a location where the electric potential is V₁ to a location where the electric potential is V₂. Which expression gives the change in the electric potential energy of the particle–field system?
options: +q·(V₂ − V₁)
+q·|V₂ − V₁|
−(V₂ − V₁)/q
−q·(V₂ − V₁)
optionWhy: A student who drops the sign of the particle's charge picks this, the change for a positive charge. The charge is −q, so ΔU_E = −q(V₂ − V₁): for a negative charge, a move to higher potential lowers U_E.
A student who uses only the size of the potential difference picks this, so that U_E always increases. Both ΔV = V₂ − V₁ and the charge have signs, and ΔU_E can be negative.

A student who rearranges ΔV = ΔU_E/q wrongly, dividing the potential difference by the charge, picks this: (V₂ − V₁)/(−q) = −(V₂ − V₁)/q. ΔU_E = qΔV, so multiply by the charge; volts divided by coulombs is not an energy.
ΔU_E = (charge)(ΔV), with the particle's charge −q and ΔV = V_final − V_initial = V₂ − V₁. So ΔU_E = −q(V₂ − V₁): if V₂ > V₁, the negative particle's electric potential energy decreases.
questions.explain: ΔU_E = (charge)(ΔV), with the particle's charge −q and ΔV = V_final − V_initial = V₂ − V₁. So ΔU_E = −q(V₂ − V₁): if V₂ > V₁, the negative particle's electric potential energy decreases.

questions.q: An electron is released from rest at a location where the electric potential is 50 V. Moving under the electric force alone, it reaches a location where the electric potential is 250 V. How much kinetic energy has it gained? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
optionWhy: The electron moves through ΔV = 250 V − 50 V = +200 V, so ΔU_E = qΔV = (−1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(200 V) = −3.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. The energy of the electron–field system is conserved, so the kinetic energy gained is ΔK = −ΔU_E = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.

A student who uses the potential at the final location, 250 V, instead of the potential difference picks this: (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(250 V). The energy change depends on the difference, 250 V − 50 V = 200 V.

A student who carries the factor 1/2 of U_C = (1/2)QΔV over to a single charge picks this: (1/2)(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(200 V). A charge moving through a fixed potential difference changes the potential energy by qΔV, with no factor of 1/2.

A student who counts both the work done by the electric force and the loss of electric potential energy picks this: 2 × 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. These are two descriptions of the same energy transfer; with the electron–field system, ΔK = −ΔU_E = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.
questions.explain: The electron moves through ΔV = 250 V − 50 V = +200 V, so ΔU_E = qΔV = (−1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(200 V) = −3.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. The energy of the electron–field system is conserved, so the kinetic energy gained is ΔK = −ΔU_E = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.
